questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Derivative of a Linear Sum of Functions
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039683/assets/cf3cc180e5489aa83c17b47db641aae68d03b095085102a29a2942a783369c07.png)

The graphs of the functions $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are given above. Find ${h}^{′}(3)$ where $h(x)=f(x)+g(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
The addition rule for derivatives gives

$$
{h}^{′}(x)={f}^{′}(x)+{g}^{′}(x).
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{h}^{′}(3)={f}^{′}(3)+{g}^{′}(3).
$$

Also, notice that $x=3$ corresponds to

- the interval $x\in (2,4)$ for the function $f,$ and

- the interval $x\in (2.5,4)$ for the function $g,$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039683/assets/19a32fa6a7b2b6481052ab3539838bb00d486f92ea3f08b54efa2a1cfc69d221.png)

- The slope of $y=f(x)$ is constant on $x\in (2,4)$ and equals

$$
\frac{Δf}{Δx}=\frac{0-2}{4-2}=-1.
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(3)=-1.$

- The slope of $y=g(x)$ is constant on $x\in (2.5,4)$ and equals

$$
\frac{Δg}{Δx}=\frac{1-1}{4-2.5}=0.
$$

Therefore, ${g}^{′}(3)=0.$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(3) & ={f}^{′}(3)+{g}^{′}(3) \\  & =-1+0 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039683/assets/c4585c2a9cf0a66da02f96a17dad5986ed8c401a844276f08b367eed765c111d.png)

The graphs of the functions $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are given above. Find ${h}^{′}(2)$ where $h(x)=f(x)-g(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
The addition and constant multiple rules for derivatives give

$$
{h}^{′}(x)={f}^{′}(x)-{g}^{′}(x).
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{h}^{′}(2)={f}^{′}(2)-{g}^{′}(2).
$$

Also, notice that $x=2$ corresponds to 

- the interval $x\in (-2,3)$ for the function $f,$ and

- the interval $x\in (-2,3)$ for the function $g,$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039683/assets/299b996bf08e4b4e8560d013829ddd1f42751767cd3f00dcd04c23c95f2c62b4.png)

- The slope of $y=f(x)$ is constant on $x\in (-2,3)$ and equals

$$
\frac{Δf}{Δx}=\frac{1-1}{3-(-2)}=0.
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(2)=0.$

- The slope of $y=g(x)$ is constant on $x\in (-2,3)$ and equals

$$
\frac{Δg}{Δx}=\frac{3-(-2)}{3-(-2)}=1.
$$

Therefore, ${g}^{′}(2)=1.$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(2) & ={f}^{′}(2)-{g}^{′}(2) \\  & =0-1 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Derivative of a Quotient of Functions
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039683/assets/931802565a13dac284496f41ebb19238402056689a96288b2fbb1dd9f018ae12.png)

Given the plots of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ above, find ${h}^{′}(-1)$ where $h(x)=\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The quotient rule for derivatives gives

$$
{h}^{′}(x)=\frac{{f}^{′}(x)\cdot g(x)-f(x)\cdot {g}^{′}(x)}{(g(x))^{2}}.
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{h}^{′}(-1)=\frac{{f}^{′}(-1)\cdot g(-1)-f(-1)\cdot {g}^{′}(-1)}{(g(-1))^{2}}.
$$

From the graph above, we obtain that $f(-1)=0$ and $g(-1)=1.$

Additionally:

- The slope of $f(x)$ on $x\in (-4,2)$ equals $\frac{2}{3}.$ So, ${f}^{′}(-1)=\frac{2}{3}.$

- The slope of $g(x)$ on $x\in (-3,2)$ equals $1.$ So, ${g}^{′}(-1)=1.$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(-1) & =\frac{{f}^{′}(-1)\cdot g(-1)-f(-1)\cdot {g}^{′}(-1)}{(g(-1))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\frac{2}{3}\cdot 1-0\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Derivative of a Product of Functions
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039683/assets/7b44dcfdfef91ada119ea7346b59f337a82bc8cca1e364fd6ea29c9eead5a2fd.png)

The graphs of the functions $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are given above. Find ${h}^{′}(-3)$ where $h(x)=f(x)g(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
The product rule for derivatives gives

$$
{h}^{′}(x)={f}^{′}(x)\cdot g(x)+f(x)\cdot {g}^{′}(x).
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{h}^{′}(-3)={f}^{′}(-3)\cdot g(-3)+f(-3)\cdot {g}^{′}(-3).
$$

From the graphs above, we obtain that $f(-3)=-2$ and $g(-3)=0.$

Additionally,

- The slope of $f(x)$ on $x\in (-4,2)$ equals $1.$ So, ${f}^{′}(-3)=1.$

- The slope of $g(x)$ on $x\in (-4,-2)$ equals $3.$ So, ${g}^{′}(-3)=3.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(-3) & ={f}^{′}(-3)\cdot g(-3)+f(-3)\cdot {g}^{′}(-3) \\  & =1\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot 3 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

The graphs of the functions $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are given above. Find ${p}^{′}(3)$ where $p(x)=f(x)g(x).$

${p}^{′}(3)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The product rule for derivatives gives

$$
{p}^{′}(x)={f}^{′}(x)\cdot g(x)+f(x)\cdot {g}^{′}(x).
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{p}^{′}(3)={f}^{′}(3)\cdot g(3)+f(3)\cdot {g}^{′}(3).
$$

From the graphs above, we obtain that $f(3)=\frac{1}{2}$ and $g(3)=1.$

Additionally,

- The slope of $f(x)$ on $x\in (2,4)$ equals $\frac{1}{2}.$ So, ${f}^{′}(3)=\frac{1}{2}.$

- The slope of $g(x)$ on $x\in (2,4)$ equals $2.$ So, ${g}^{′}(3)=2.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{′}(3) & ={f}^{′}(3)\cdot g(3)+f(3)\cdot {g}^{′}(3) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2})\cdot 1+(\frac{1}{2})\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
